For every ε > 0 there is C(ε) such that for all X ≥ 2,
N(X) = #{1 ≤ n ≤ X : n is 2-full and n+1 is 3-full} ≤ C(ε) X^{3/10+ε}.

targets.statement: There is no integer n > 0 such that n is 2-full and n+1 is 3-full. Equivalently, for all cube-free k ≥ 1 and u ≥ 2 with rad(k) | u, k u³ − 1 is not powerful.

For every cube-free k ≥ 1 and every s ≥ 1 with k·s ≤ 10^5, the equation k u³ − s² t³ = 1 has no positive solution with rad(k) | u. Hence no solution n = s²t³ (with any t ≥ 1, and n of any size) has k·s ≤ 10^5. In particular, u³ − 1 = s²t³ has no solution with s ≤ 10^5 and any u.

There is an absolute δ > 0 such that for every cube-free k ≥ 1, the squarefree t ≤ T with gcd(t,k)=1 and rank E_{k,t}(Q) = 0 number at least δ·#{squarefree t ≤ T, gcd(t,k)=1} for T ≥ T₀(k). Every such fibre (k,t) contains no solution. Also give an explicit δ₁ for k = 1.
Every fibre (k,t) with k cube-free, t squarefree, gcd(k,t)=1 and k·t ≤ 10^4 contains no solution. That is, Y² = X³ − k²t³ has no integral point with X = ktu, Y = kt³s, s ≥ 1, rad(k) | u.
Assume Baker's explicit abc conjecture: c < (6/5)·r·(log r)^ω/ω!, where r = rad(abc) and ω = ω(abc). Then there is no n > 0 with n 2-full and n+1 3-full.
For every integer u ≥ 2, u³ − 1 is not powerful. This is the k = 1 case: n+1 is a perfect cube.

- (a) The system k u³ − s²t³ = 1, rad(k) | u, t squarefree has nonzero integer solutions (1,−2,3,−1) and (1,−23,39,−2). - (b) Consequently, no argument whose input is invariant under the sign change (t,u) → (−t,−u) can prove T1. This covers: - local solubility at all finite places; - Brauer–Manin on the total space; - class-group or Selmer conditions depending only on the squarefree part of t up t

Suppose n+1 = p^a with p prime and a ≥ 3 (respectively n = p^a, a ≥ 2) in a solution. Then there is a prime q (the largest prime factor of a; q odd in the second case) such that the primitive part Φ*_q(p) (respectively Φ*_{2q}(p)) is powerful (respectively cube-full), and every prime factor r of it satisfies r² | p^{r−1} − 1. - Corollary 1: n+1 = 2^a is impossible unless some Mersenne number M_q (

In the random model where n is 2-full and n+1 is 3-full independently with their exact local densities, conditioned on gcd(n,n+1)=1, the expected number of solutions with n > X is (κ+o(1))X^{-1/6}. Here κ = 6·(ζ(3/2)/2ζ(3))·(c₃/3)·∏_p E_p, with explicit local correction factors E_p. Moreover: - the same model for the mirrored problem predicts about the observed 2 solutions (8, 12167) below 10^24;
For all integers k ≥ 2, n ≥ 0, m ≥ n+k: ∏_{i=1}^k (m+i) ≠ 4·∏_{i=1}^k (n+i). Hence the Lean statement erdos_686 is false, with witness N = 4.

The integer solutions of X³−X = 4(Y³−Y) are exactly {−1,0,1}² ∪ {±(3,2)}. Consequently F_3(m) = 4F_3(n) with m > n ≥ 0 only for (n,m) = (0,1). By the symmetry, 4 has no representation with k = 3, and none with m−n = 3.
For 2 ≤ t ≤ 100, t² is 3-representable (k = 3, m ≥ n+3) iff t ∈ {3, 4, 70}.

Let C₅: P(X) = 4P(Y), with P = x⁵−5x³+4x, X = m+3, Y = n+3, and ι(X,Y) = (−X,−Y). Let A = (1−ι)J(C₅), the 4-dimensional Prym. If rank A(Q) ≤ 3, then C₅(Q) = {−2,…,2}² ∪ {±(14/3, 11/3)}. Hence 4 is not 5-representable, and has no representation with m−n = 5.
Assume the abc conjecture. Then 4 is not representable, i.e. T1 holds.
For N = 4, every k ≥ 3, and m ≥ n+k with F_k(m) = 4F_k(n): s = n+k ≥ k³/100.

Let k ≥ 3 be odd, α = 4^(1/k), c_k = (k²−1)(α⁻¹−α)/24, and X = m+(k+1)/2, Y = n+(k+1)/2 with F_k(m) = 4F_k(n) and Y ≥ k². - Then |Y(X−αY) − c_k| ≤ C·k⁴/Y² for an explicit absolute C. - Hence, with p/q = X/Y in lowest terms, (p,q) = (r·p_{j+1} ± s·p_j, r·q_{j+1} ± s·q_j) for convergents p_j/q_j of α and integers r, s ≥ 0 with rs < 2|c_k|+1 ≈ 0.23k. This is Worley's theorem.

For every q ≥ 2, k ≥ 2, n ≥ 0, m ≥ n+k: if N = ∏(q^{m+i}−1)/∏(q^{n+i}−1) is an integer, then N has at least k−1 distinct prime factors ≡ 1 (mod m+i). In particular no N ≤ 2^{k} and no power of 2 is q-representable.
The anti-invariant class [P − ιP] with P = (14/3, 11/3) ∈ C₅(Q) has infinite order. Hence rank J(C₅)(Q) ≥ 6 = genus, and classical Chabauty–Coleman on C₅ cannot work.

Write F_k(a) = (a+1)⋯(a+k). For all n ≥ 0 and k, d ≥ 1, F_k(n+d)/F_k(n) = F_d(n+k)/F_d(n). Hence: - 4 is not representable ⇐ [for every a ∈ A and every b ≥ a, F_a(n+b) ≠ 4F_a(n)], where A = {odd a ≥ 3} ∪ {even a ≥ 342}. This uses the harness even-k result, which covers all gaps. - In that remaining case, s ≥ max(a³/10⁴, a·b/ln 4·(1−o(1))).
For every finite A ⊂ ℤ_{≥2} and all integers m > n ≥ max A: F(m)/m < 2F(n)/n.

Let A be primitive, n ≥ max A, L′ = A∩(n/4,n], A_s = A∖L′. For a∈L′ let D_a = {a′/gcd(a,a′) : a′ ∈ A_s ∪ {a″∈L′ : a″>a}} and N_D(y) = #{k≤y : no d∈D divides k}. - (a) F_A(x) = F_{A_s}(x) + Σ_{a∈L′} N_{D_a}(x/a) for all x. - (b) For m>n, N_{D_a}(m/a)/m < 2N_{D_a}(n/a)/n for every a∈L′. Consequences: - Every counterexample (A,n,m) yields a counterexample (A_s,n,m) with A_s ⊂ [3,n/4] nonempty and pri
The inequality holds for every A with |A|=4. Stretch goal: |A|=5.
For every finite set A of primes and n ≥ max A: 1−∏_{p∈A}(1−1/p) < 2F_A(n)/n. This is the m→∞ case with the sharp constant.
The inequality holds whenever min A > n/8. With C=23 in place of 8 this yields T3; with C=47 it yields |A|=5.
There is an absolute C (any explicit value) such that for every finite A and all m > n ≥ max A: F(m)/m ≤ C·F(n)/n.
For every finite A and n ≥ max A: d(A) < 2F(n)/n. This is the m→∞ form, Tao's "cheat 1" alone.

Assume WP, a restricted form of the blackboard's peelability conjecture: for every primitive A ⊂ [3,n/4] with F_A(n) < n/2 and every m>n, some a∈A satisfies π_a(m)/m ≤ 2π_a(n)/n. Here π_a counts multiples of a divisible by no other element. Then erdős_488 holds.

Let W_n(A) = max_{x≥0} |B∩(x,x+n]|. If W_n(A) < 2F_A(n) for all primitive A ⊂ [3,n/4] (window inequality X), then T7 holds. Proof: - Averaging over one period gives Σ_{x=0}^{L−1} |B∩(x,x+n]| = nLd, so W_n ≥ nd. - T2 passes to the limit with strictness.

Continuous prime-scale model. For measurable E ⊂ (0,1) let μ = ∫_E du/u and Ψ(E) = Σ_j ((−1)^j/j!) ∫_{E^j ∩ {Σu_i ≤ 1}} ∏ du_i/u_i, and set R(E) = (1−e^{−μ})/(1−Ψ(E)). Determine sup_E R(E), and prove sup R ≤ 1.1, or find E with R(E) > 1.1.

The precise statement. For every C>0 there is ε>0 such that for all large n and all x ∈ [−1,1]^n there is y ∈ [−1,1]^n such that every real polynomial P with deg P < (1+ε)n and P(x_i)=y_i for ≥ (1−ε)n indices has max_{[−1,1]}|P| > C.

Fix a density f on [−1,1] that is bounded and positive on a subinterval. For every C there is ε = ε(C,f) > 0 such that, if x_1..x_n are i.i.d. from f, then with probability → 1 there exists y with the property in T1.
T1 holds for the Chebyshev nodes x_i = cos((2i−1)π/2n), with y_i = (−1)^i·s_{⌊iε/δ⌋}, where s is the alternating block sign, δ = 1/10 and ε ≤ δ·e^{−AC} for an absolute constant A.

For the circle, with N equispaced points θ_j = 2πj/N: for every C there is ε such that there exists y ∈ [−1,1]^N such that every real trigonometric polynomial of degree < (1+ε)N/2 matching y at ≥ (1−ε)N points has sup > C.

Hypothesis (KEY): there are γ(C) > 0 and η_0(C) > 0 such that for every multiset of k nodes in [−1,1], every m ≤ (1+η_0)k, and y uniform in {±1}^k, Pr[∃P with deg P ≤ m, ‖P‖ ≤ C, P(x_i)=y_i ∀i] ≤ e^{−γk}. Then T1 holds. Proof sketch: take a union bound over S with |S| = ⌈(1−ε)n⌉, which gives ≤ e^{H(ε)n} subsets; note m < (1+ε)n ≤ (1+3ε)|S|; choose ε with H(ε) < γ/2 and 3ε ≤ η_0.

KEY (from T5) holds for subsets of size ≥ (1−3ε)n of the Chebyshev nodes: random ±1 data on such a subset is interpolable by degree ≤ (1+3ε)n with norm ≤ C with probability ≤ e^{−γ(C)n}, where γ does not depend on ε ≤ ε_0(C).

Any valid ε(C) in T1, and already in Erdős's full-interpolation theorem, satisfies ε(C) ≤ exp(−cC) for an absolute c > 0. Witness: Chebyshev nodes, where discrete de la Vallée Poussin interpolation of degree (1+η)n has norm ≤ A·log(1/η) + A.
Erdős's full-interpolation theorem holds with ε(C) = exp(−AC) for an absolute A. Together with T8 this pins log(1/ε(C)) ≍ C.

Assume the AE lemma (T6) and the near-Chebyshev case of KEY: KEY for node sets θ-separated by c/k with arcsine discrepancy ≤ 3εk on all arcs. Then T1 holds. (No standard named conjecture such as GRH or abc bears on this analytic problem.)
k(N) − (e−1)N → ∞ as N → ∞ (the Lean statement erdos_295).

k(N) ≤ (e−1)N + O(log N). Proof plan: - Let M be maximal with Σ_{n=N}^{M} 1/n < 1. Then M − N + 1 = (e−1)N + O(1). - The remainder ρ = a/b has b | lcm(N..M), so log log b ≤ log N + O(1). - [025] writes ρ as O(log log b) distinct unit fractions. - Each of them is ≤ ρ ≤ 1/(M+1), so all are new and distinct from the interval.

Strengthen the KNOWN structure lemma as follows. If |S| ≤ (e−1)N + C, then all but o(π(eN)) primes p ∈ [N^{1/2+ε},(1−δ)eN] divide an element of S above (1+δ)eN. Consequently ∏_{far} n ≥ exp((e − O(δ) − o(1))N). For r = 1 the far element b satisfies b | lcm(S'), b ≡ −p/H_p (mod p²), and b ≥ lcm(S')·e^{−O(δN)}.

For each C there is N₀(C) such that for N ≥ N₀ no representation 1 = Σ_S 1/n with S ⊂ [N,∞) and |S| ≤ (e−1)N + C has exactly one element exceeding 3N. That is, the case r = 1: the numerator of 1 − Σ_{S'} 1/n is never 1 for near-interval S' ⊂ [N,3N].
Let k_X(N) be k(N) with all denominators ≤ X. For N² ≤ X ≤ exp(N/log N): k_X(N) − (e−1)N = Θ(N/log X).

Assume Hypothesis H, defined as follows. For every fixed r, and every rational ρ = a/D whose reduced denominator is divisible by at least half the primes of [N,2N], if ρ is a sum of r distinct unit fractions then a ≥ D·exp(−o(N)). Then CORE holds. No standard named conjecture (GRH, abc, Hypothesis H of Schinzel) is known to us to imply CORE. H is a non-standard, "typical-numerator Erdős–Graham" ty
For every R, the set {N : k(N) ≤ (e−1)N + R} has natural density 0.
For all large N and any θ > 1/2, there are S' (near-interval) and at most 3 integers b_j > eN such that Σ_{S'} 1/n + Σ_j 1/b_j has reduced denominator free of primes > N^θ.
For every strictly increasing A ⊂ ℕ_{>0} and every ε > 0 there is k such that F(A,X,k) < X^ε for all X > 0. Equivalently, F(A,X,k) ≪_{ε} X^ε for k ≥ k(ε).

Write CDC_sq for: for every θ < 1/2 there is K(θ) such that every perfect square N satisfies #{d | N : |d − √N| ≤ N^θ} ≤ K(θ). Then CDC_sq implies T1, quantitatively: F(A,X,k) ≤ 2k(X^ε + 1)(log₂X + 1) for k > K(1/2 − ε/2). Proof: 1. Blocks with relative spread ≥ X^{−ε} are handled by packing over dyadic heights. 2. For any other block d_1 < … < d_k with lcm L < X, the integers e_i = d_i·L/d_1 divi

(i) Let T ⊂ ℤ with |T| = U, and suppose k distinct s-subsets of T share p_1,…,p_r. Then some strictly increasing A satisfies F(A,X,k) ≥ c_T X^{(r+1)/(U+r+1)} for arbitrarily large X. The same holds for pools of pairwise non-associate integral linear forms in several variables. (ii) Let M(c) be the supremum of such k over all integer pools with r ≥ c|T|. Then TRUE implies M(c) < ∞ for every c > 0.

For every ε > 0 there is K(ε) such that every n with ω(n) ≤ 3 and every y > 0 satisfy #{d | n : y ≤ d ≤ y(1+n^{−ε})} ≤ K(ε). Consequently, for k > K(ε/2) and every A, #{i : lcm(a_i,…,a_{i+k−1}) < X, ω(lcm) ≤ 3} ≪ X^ε log X. Stretch: the same for ω(n) ≤ s, with K(s,ε).
There is k with F(A,X,k) ≪ X^{1/4} for every strictly increasing A, with no ε and no log factor.
There exist η > 0 and k with F(A,X,k) ≪ X^{1/4−η} for every A.
Assume Vojta's Main Conjecture with truncated counting functions, for blow-ups of ℙ^{k−1} over ℚ along the diagonal arrangement {x_i = x_j}. Then T1 holds.

For every c > 0 there is K_ℂ(c) with the following property. If L ∈ ℂ[t] has degree N and P_1,…,P_k are distinct monic divisors of L of equal degree with deg(P_i − P_j) ≤ deg P_i − cN for all i, j, then k ≤ K_ℂ(c). The analogue over F_q[t] with q fixed is false (BARRIERS).

Suppose a one-variable pool T (linear factors x+t) gives k divisors in relative window n^{−ε}. Then diam(T) ≥ c(ε|T|)² and |T| ≥ log₂ k. In particular, pools of diameter ≤ C|T| force k ≤ 2^{C'/ε²}. This matches r1s3 up to the log factor, so k(ε) = exp(Θ̃(1/ε²)) within dense polynomial families.

∀ c > 0, ∃ᶠ n in atTop, ∃ X : Finset ℝ², #X = n ∧ IsValid X ∧ distinctDistances X < (1+c)n/2. Explicitly, for every n ≥ 3 the vertex set of the regular n-gon is valid and determines exactly ⌊n/2⌋ nonzero distances.
If n = 2k+1 ≥ 5, X is valid and D(X) = k, then X is the vertex set of a regular n-gon.
There is a c > 0 such that every convex-position valid X with no four concyclic points has D(X) ≥ (1+c)n/2. More strongly, convex valid X with D ≤ (1+δ)n/2 has ≥ (1−ε)n points concyclic.
Let X be valid and contained in the union of two circles (or a circle and a line), with each part of size ≥ εn. Then D(X) ≥ (1+c(ε))n/2.
Every valid X with no four concyclic points has D(X) ≥ n/2 + f(n) for some f(n) → ∞, for instance f(n) = c·log n.
CORE (S). For every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that every valid X with D ≤ (1+δ)n/2 has ≥ (1−ε)n concyclic points.

Let I(X) be the number of apex-labelled isosceles triangles (x; {y,z}) with |xy| = |xz|. For valid X, D(X) ≥ n − 1 − I(X)/n. Hence the general-position version of #655 follows from the claim: (R) Every valid X with no 3 collinear and no 4 concyclic satisfies I(X) ≤ (1/2 − η)n², i.e. the average number of apexes per pair is ≤ 1 − 2η. Proof of the implication: point x sees n − 1 − s₂(x) distances, w
Assume the linear form of Erdős #98: h(n) ≥ (1/2 + η)n for sets with no 3 collinear and no 4 concyclic. Then every valid X with no 4 concyclic (collinear triples allowed) has D(X) ≥ (1/2 + η′)n.

Let f_k(n) be the minimum of D(X) over n-point sets X in which every circle centred at a point of X contains ≤ k other points. Then f_3(n) ≥ (1/2 − o(1))n, or else an explicit family achieves f_3(n) ≤ (1/2 − δ)n.
Let X = A ∪ B be valid, where A is concyclic, B is disjoint from the circle, and 1 ≤ |B| ≤ K. Then D(X) ≥ (1+c)n/2 for n ≥ n₀(K). For K = 1, D(X) ≥ n − O(1) when A is a regular polygon.
